almohad-caliphate.name: Almohad Caliphate
almohad-caliphate.summary: North African empire ruled by a Berber Muslim dynasty in the 12th and 13th centuries, controlling much of the Maghreb and Islamic Spain at its height.

al-andalus.name: Al-Andalus
al-andalus.summary: The Muslim-ruled territories of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to 1492, which at their height covered all of Spain and Portugal, with Córdoba becoming a leading cultural and scientific center.

makroudh.name: Makroudh
makroudh.summary: Diamond-shaped Maghrebi cookie made from semolina dough and filled with dates and nuts or almond paste, fried or baked.

daniel-newman-academic.name: Daniel Newman
daniel-newman-academic.summary: British writer, scholar and translator of Arabic literature (1963–2026), a former advisor to Durham Law School's Islamic Criminal Justice Project.

ibn-raz-n-al-tuj-b.name: Ibn Razin al-Tujibi
ibn-raz-n-al-tuj-b.summary: A 13th-century Muslim Andalusi scholar, born in Murcia in 1227, whose cookbook is one of only two to survive from that era; he wrote it around 1260 while living in Tunis.

hippocrates.name: Hippocrates
hippocrates.summary: A Greek physician and philosopher (c. 460–370 BC) traditionally called the 'Father of Medicine' for pioneering prognosis and clinical observation, and credited with the Hippocratic Oath.

galen.name: Galen
galen.summary: A Roman-era Greek physician, surgeon, and philosopher (129–c.216 CE) whose anatomical writings, shaped by the four-humors theory, dominated Western medicine for over 1,300 years.

banu-hilal.name: Banu Hilal
banu-hilal.summary: An Arab tribe from Najd, part of which the Fatimids sent westward into the Maghreb in the 11th century to punish the Zirids.

banu-sulaym.name: Banu Sulaym
banu-sulaym.summary: An Arab tribe from the Hejaz that fought Muhammad before converting to Islam, later migrating westward with the Banu Hilal into Libya's Cyrenaica.

sfenj.name: Sfenj
sfenj.summary: A light, spongy Maghrebi doughnut fried in oil, traditionally eaten for breakfast plain, sugared or soaked in honey.

tabil.name: Tabil
tabil.summary: A Tunisian spice mixture of ground coriander, caraway, garlic and chili, often combined with harissa in stews and vegetable dishes.

paula-wolfert.name: Paula Wolfert
paula-wolfert.summary: American cookbook author and specialist in Mediterranean food, particularly Moroccan cuisine, winner of the James Beard Foundation's lifetime achievement medal.

solomon-ibn-verga.name: Solomon ibn Verga
solomon-ibn-verga.summary: A Spanish-born Sephardic Jewish historian, physician and author (c. 1460–1554), nephew of Judah ibn Verga, who wrote the Shevet Yehudah ('Scepter of Judah').

h-l-ne-jawhara-pi-er.name: Hélène Jawhara Piñer
h-l-ne-jawhara-pi-er.summary: French-Spanish historian, educator and chef specializing in Sephardic cuisine and medieval Jewish food culture in Spain and France, who has lectured and hosted a cooking show on the subject.

mofletta.name: mofletta
mofletta.summary: A thin Maghrebi Jewish crêpe made from water, flour and oil, traditionally served warm with butter, honey or jam during the Mimouna celebration held after Passover.

riad-architecture.name: Riad
riad-architecture.summary: A garden courtyard divided into four quadrants around a central fountain, historically part of house and palace architecture in the Maghreb and al-Andalus, likely derived from Persian gardens.

almoravid-dynasty.name: Almoravid dynasty
almoravid-dynasty.summary: Berber Muslim dynasty (1050s-1147) centered in Morocco that built an empire across the western Maghreb and Muslim Spain, founding Marrakesh around 1070.

ali-ibn-yusuf.name: Ali ibn Yusuf
ali-ibn-yusuf.summary: Almoravid emir who ruled from 1106 to 1143, succeeding his father Yusuf ibn Tashfin, and led campaigns against Christian kingdoms in Iberia while facing new Muslim rivals.

fez-morocco.name: Fez
fez-morocco.summary: A city in northern Morocco founded in the 8th century, which became a center of religious scholarship and reached its height under Marinid rule in the 13th to 15th centuries.

tlemcen.name: Tlemcen
tlemcen.summary: The second-largest city in northwestern Algeria, a historic center of the Maghreb blending Arab, Berber, Andalusi, and Ottoman influences.

zellij.name: Zellij
zellij.summary: A North African style of mosaic tilework made of hand-chiseled tiles forming geometric patterns, a hallmark of architecture in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and al-Andalus since the 14th century.

marinid-dynasty.name: Marinid dynasty
marinid-dynasty.summary: A Berber dynasty that ruled much of the Maghreb, chiefly Morocco, from the mid-13th to the 15th century, at its height also holding parts of Algeria, Tunisia and southern Spain.

tashfiniya-madrasa.name: Tashfiniya Madrasa
tashfiniya-madrasa.summary: A former Islamic school in Tlemcen, Algeria, built in the early 14th century by Zayyanid ruler Abu Tashfin I and noted for its rich decoration before its demolition in 1876.

abu-tashfin-abd-al-rahman-i.name: Abu Tashfin Abd al-Rahman I
abu-tashfin-abd-al-rahman-i.summary: Zayyanid sultan of Tlemcen who overthrew his own father in 1318, captured Algiers and Tunis from the Hafsids in 1329, and was killed by the Marinids and Hafsids during a siege in 1337.

zayyanid-dynasty.name: Zayyanid dynasty
zayyanid-dynasty.summary: A Berber Zenata dynasty, also called the Abd al-Wadids, that ruled the Kingdom of Tlemcen in modern Algeria from 1235 to 1557.

great-mosque-of-tlemcen.name: Great Mosque of Tlemcen
great-mosque-of-tlemcen.summary: A mosque in Tlemcen, Algeria, first built in 1082 and considered a major example of Almoravid architecture, later extended under the Zayyanid dynasty.

sidi-belahcen-mosque.name: Sidi Belahcen Mosque
sidi-belahcen-mosque.summary: Former mosque in Tlemcen, Algeria, next to the Great Mosque of Tlemcen, now repurposed as the National Public Museum of Islamic Calligraphy.

great-mosque-of-constantine.name: Great Mosque of Constantine
great-mosque-of-constantine.summary: A Sunni mosque in Constantine, Algeria, originally built by the Hammadids in the 12th century on the ruins of a Roman temple.

hammadid-dynasty.name: Hammadid dynasty
hammadid-dynasty.summary: A medieval Islamic kingdom in the central Maghreb, founded in the early 11th century, which at its height stretched from Tlemcen to Tunis.

abu-yaqub-yusuf-an-nasr.name: Abu Yaqub Yusuf an-Nasr
abu-yaqub-yusuf-an-nasr.summary: Marinid ruler who succeeded his father Abu Yusuf Ya'qub in 1286 and was assassinated in 1307.

hafsid-dynasty.name: Hafsid dynasty
hafsid-dynasty.summary: A Sunni Muslim dynasty of Berber descent that ruled Ifriqiya, roughly modern Tunisia, western Libya and eastern Algeria, from 1229 to 1574, with Tunis as its capital.

fatimid-caliphate.name: Fatimid Caliphate
fatimid-caliphate.summary: An Isma'ili Shia caliphate ruling North Africa and West Asia from the 10th to 12th centuries CE, claiming descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima, with Egypt as its eventual centre.

zirid-dynasty.name: Zirid dynasty
zirid-dynasty.summary: A Sanhaja Berber dynasty that ruled the central Maghreb from 972 to 1014 and Ifriqiya until 1148, at first as emirs governing in the name of the Fatimid Caliphate.

eighth-crusade.name: Eighth Crusade
eighth-crusade.summary: A 1270 crusade led by Louis IX of France against the Hafsid dynasty in Tunisia; Louis died of dysentery shortly after arriving, and little fighting took place.

muhammad-i-al-mustansir.name: Muhammad I al-Mustansir
muhammad-i-al-mustansir.summary: Second Sultan of Ifriqiya of the Hafsid dynasty, living around 1228 to 1277 and the first to claim the title of caliph; he made peace to end the Eighth Crusade in 1270.

battle-of-haydaran.name: Battle of Haydaran
battle-of-haydaran.summary: An 1052 battle in what is now south-east Tunisia in which the Arab Banu Hilal defeated the Zirid dynasty, forcing the Zirids to abandon Kairouan for the coast.

kairouan.name: Kairouan
kairouan.summary: City in Tunisia founded by the Umayyads around 670, which became an important center of Sunni Islamic scholarship and Quranic learning.

zenata.name: Zenata
zenata.summary: A group of nomadic or semi-nomadic Berber tribes, one of the largest Berber confederations alongside the Sanhaja and Masmuda.

ifriqiya.name: Ifriqiya
ifriqiya.summary: A medieval historical region covering today's Tunisia, eastern Algeria and western Libya, whose capital was Qayrawan for most of its history.

qal-at-bani-hammad.name: Qal'at Bani Hammad
qal-at-bani-hammad.summary: A now-ruined fortified palatine city in Algeria that served as the first capital of the Hammadid dynasty in the 11th century, today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

constantine-algeria.name: Constantine
constantine-algeria.summary: Capital of Constantine Province in northeastern Algeria, known as Cirta in Roman times before being renamed after Emperor Constantine the Great; nicknamed the 'City of Bridges'.

abd-al-mu-min.name: Abd al-Mu'min
abd-al-mu-min.summary: Founder of the Almohad ruling dynasty and empire, who became its first caliph in 1133 and extended its rule across the Maghreb and Al-Andalus until his death in 1163.

kabyle-people.name: Kabyle people
kabyle-people.summary: Berber ethnic group indigenous to Kabylia in northern Algeria, the largest Berber population in Algeria, with a large diaspora especially in France.

barghawata.name: Barghawata
barghawata.summary: A Berber tribal confederation and religious movement that ruled Morocco's Atlantic coast from the 8th to 11th centuries, after allying with a rebellion against the Umayyad Caliphate.

ibn-khaldun.name: Ibn Khaldun
ibn-khaldun.summary: An Arab Tunisian scholar and historian (1332–1406), best known for the Muqaddimah, a foundational work in historiography, sociology and economics.

abu-zayd-al-hilali.name: Abu Zayd al-Hilali
abu-zayd-al-hilali.summary: 11th-century Arab leader and legendary hero of the Banu Hilal who, on Fatimid orders, led his tribe into Ifriqiya to punish the Zirids, sacking Kairouan in the process.

moulouya-river.name: Moulouya River
moulouya-river.summary: A 520-km river in Morocco running from the Middle Atlas to the Mediterranean, used today for irrigation.

doukkala.name: Doukkala
doukkala.summary: A fertile plain region of Morocco, now part of the Casablanca-Settat administrative area, known mainly for agriculture.

one-hundred-and-one-nights-book.name: One Hundred and One Nights
one-hundred-and-one-nights-book.summary: Collection of twenty Arabic stories resembling the more famous One Thousand and One Nights, likely originating in the Maghreb; its oldest known manuscript, found in 2010, dates to 1234 or 1235.

rawd-al-qirtas.name: Rawd al-Qirtas
rawd-al-qirtas.summary: A 14th-century book describing the rulers of the Maghreb and the history of Fez, usually attributed to Ibn Abi Zar, though its authorship remains uncertain.

ibn-abi-zar.name: Ibn Abi Zar
ibn-abi-zar.summary: A scholar at Fes, who died between 1310 and 1320, commonly presumed to be the author of the influential medieval Maghreb history Rawd al-Qirtas.

abu-sa-id-uthman-ii.name: Abu Sa'id Uthman II
abu-sa-id-uthman-ii.summary: Ninth Marinid sultan (1276-1331), reigning from 1310, who succeeded his nephew as ruler at age 33.

simeon-ben-zemah-duran.name: Simeon ben Zemah Duran
simeon-ben-zemah-duran.summary: Jewish scholar and rabbinic authority, 1361–1444, who fled Spain for Algeria after the 1391 pogroms and became rabbinic leader of Algerian Jewry in 1408.

claudia-ott.name: Claudia Ott
claudia-ott.summary: German scholar of Middle-Eastern languages and musician, best known for her 2004 translation from the oldest surviving Arabic manuscript of One Thousand and One Nights.

scheherazade.name: Scheherazade
scheherazade.summary: Legendary narrator of One Thousand and One Nights, who saves herself and other women by telling King Shahryar interlinked stories over 1,001 nights, gradually transforming him into a just ruler.

the-ebony-horse.name: The Ebony Horse
the-ebony-horse.summary: Arabian Nights folk tale of a flying mechanical horse controlled by keys, used by the Prince of Persia in adventures across Persia, Arabia and Byzantium.

ibn-al-yasamin.name: Ibn al-Yasamin
ibn-al-yasamin.summary: A Maghrebi mathematician born in Fez who died in 1204, known for developing Ghubari (West Arabic) numerals now used in most of the world, and also noted for his work in literature and law.

ibn-al-banna-al-marrakushi.name: Ibn al-Banna' al-Marrakushi
ibn-al-banna-al-marrakushi.summary: A Moroccan Arab polymath (1256–1321) active as a mathematician, astronomer, Islamic scholar, Sufi and astrologer.

kutubiyya-mosque.name: Kutubiyya Mosque
kutubiyya-mosque.summary: The largest mosque in Marrakesh, Morocco, founded in 1147 by the Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min and rebuilt around 1158; its 77-metre minaret is a landmark of Almohad architecture.

ibn-zuhr.name: Ibn Zuhr
ibn-zuhr.summary: An Arab physician, surgeon and poet from Seville (1094–1162), regarded as the most well-regarded physician of his era for his rational, evidence-based approach to medicine.

ibn-tumart.name: Ibn Tumart
ibn-tumart.summary: A Muslim religious scholar and teacher from southern Morocco (c. 1080–1130) who founded the Almohad movement and led a revolt against the ruling Almoravids.

mahdi.name: Mahdi
mahdi.summary: An Islamic messianic figure expected to appear before the End Times to restore justice alongside Jesus; central to Shia theology, where he is identified with the twelfth Imam, born in 869 CE and in occultation.

tinmel.name: Tinmel
tinmel.summary: A small village in Morocco's High Atlas mountains that served as the base from which the Almohad movement launched its 12th-century conquests.

madrasa-of-abu-al-hasan.name: Abu al-Hasan
madrasa-of-abu-al-hasan.summary: 14th-century Marinid sultan who built a richly decorated madrasa next to the Grand Mosque of Salé, Morocco.

abu-inan-faris.name: Abu Inan Faris
abu-inan-faris.summary: Marinid ruler (1329-1358) who succeeded his father in 1348 and extended his rule over Tlemcen and Ifriqiya, before being strangled by his own vizier.

hammad-ibn-buluggin.name: Hammad ibn Buluggin
hammad-ibn-buluggin.summary: First ruler of the Hammadid dynasty in what is now Algeria, reigning from 1014 until his death in 1029.

nasir-ibn-alnas.name: an-Nasir ibn Alnas
nasir-ibn-alnas.summary: Fifth ruler of the Hammadid dynasty in Algeria, reigning from 1062 until his death in 1088.

battle-of-sagrajas.name: Battle of Sagrajas
battle-of-sagrajas.summary: A battle fought on 23 October 1086 between the Almoravid army under Yusuf ibn Tashfin, aided by Muslim taifa princes, and King Alfonso VI of Castile; the Almoravid win helped halt Christian expansion in Iberia.

b-ja-a.name: Béjaïa
b-ja-a.summary: A Mediterranean port city in Algeria, now capital of Béjaïa Province, built up from a small fishing village into a fortified town by the Hammadid emir al-Nasir starting in 1067.

buluggin-ibn-muhammad.name: Buluggin ibn Muhammad
buluggin-ibn-muhammad.summary: Ruler of the Hammadids from 1055 to 1062, who led an army into Morocco against the Almoravids and briefly captured Fes.

zawi-ibn-ziri.name: Zawi ibn Ziri
zawi-ibn-ziri.summary: A Berber Sanhaja chief who arrived in Spain around 1000, joined the rebellion against the Caliphate of Córdoba, and became the first emir of Granada, reigning from 1013 to 1019.

taifa-of-granada.name: Taifa of Granada
taifa-of-granada.summary: A Muslim kingdom centred on Granada in Islamic Spain, ruled by an offshoot of the Zirid dynasty from 1013 until conquered by the Almoravids in 1090.

yaghmurasen-ibn-zyan.name: Yaghmurasen ibn Zyan
yaghmurasen-ibn-zyan.summary: Founder of the Zayyanid dynasty (1206 to 1283), whose Kingdom of Tlemcen extended over present-day north-western Algeria.

alfonso-x-of-castile.name: Alfonso X of Castile
alfonso-x-of-castile.summary: King of Castile, León and Galicia from 1252 to 1284, nicknamed the Wise, who sponsored the Alfonsine astronomical tables and issued Castile's first law code written in the vernacular.

yusuf-ibn-tashfin.name: Yusuf ibn Tashfin
yusuf-ibn-tashfin.summary: Sanhaja leader of the Almoravid Empire (r. c. 1061–1106) who cofounded Marrakesh and led Muslim forces to victory at the Battle of Sagrajas against Alfonso VI.

abdallah-ibn-buluggin.name: Abdallah ibn Buluggin
abdallah-ibn-buluggin.summary: Grandson of Badis ben Habus and the last Zirid ruler of the Taifa of Granada, reigning from 1073 to 1090.

aghmat.name: Aghmat
aghmat.summary: A medieval Berber commercial town in Morocco, now an archaeological site southeast of Marrakesh, first recorded as conquered by Muslim forces in 683.

al-mu-tamid-ibn-abbad.name: al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad
al-mu-tamid-ibn-abbad.summary: Third and last ruler of the Taifa of Seville, reigning about 1069 to 1091, and a renowned poet, deposed by the Almoravids in 1091.

alfonso-vi-of-le-n-and-castile.name: Alfonso VI of León and Castile
alfonso-vi-of-le-n-and-castile.summary: King of León, Galicia and Castile who conquered Toledo in 1085, expanding his realm before spending his later reign resisting an Almoravid invasion.
alfonso-vi-of-le-n-and-castile.source_title: Alfonso VI of León and Castile

al-mu-izz-ibn-badis.name: al-Mu'izz ibn Badis
al-mu-izz-ibn-badis.summary: Fourth ruler of the Zirid dynasty in Ifriqiya, reigning 1016 to 1062, initially under the regency of his aunt Saïda bint Mansur.

ismailism.name: Ismailism
ismailism.summary: A denomination of Shia Islam, one of three alongside Twelver and Zaydi Islam, marked by its distinctive emphasis on the esoteric, hidden meaning of Islamic teaching.

al-hakim-bi-amr-allah.name: Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah
al-hakim-bi-amr-allah.summary: Sixth Fatimid caliph and sixteenth Ismaili imam (985-1021), a deeply controversial ruler seen by some as a tyrant and by others as an ideal, divinely ordained sovereign.

abd-al-haqq-ii.name: Abd al-Haqq II
abd-al-haqq-ii.summary: Marinid Sultan who ruled from 1420 to 1465.

wattasid-dynasty.name: Wattasid dynasty
wattasid-dynasty.summary: A Moroccan ruling dynasty of Zenata Berber descent that rose from viziers serving the Marinids to sultans after 1465, ruling until overthrown by the Saadi dynasty in 1554.

al-kindi.name: Al-Kindi
al-kindi.summary: A Mesopotamian Arab polymath (c. 801-873) hailed as the 'father of Arab philosophy,' who oversaw the translation of Greek texts at Baghdad's House of Wisdom and wrote on subjects from mathematics to medicine.

averroes.name: Averroes (Ibn Rushd)
averroes.summary: Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), known in the West as Averroes, was an Andalusian polymath and jurist whose commentaries on Aristotle and defence of philosophy within Islam made him influential in Europe.

muqaddimah.name: Muqaddimah
muqaddimah.summary: A 14th-century Arabic treatise by Ibn Khaldun on historiography, sociology and the philosophy of history, written in 1377 and sometimes seen as an early work of social science.

masmuda.name: Masmuda
masmuda.summary: A Berber tribal confederation, one of the largest in the Maghreb, based mainly in present-day Morocco and related to the Schleuh people.

abu-al-hasan-al-ash-ari.name: al-Ash'ari
abu-al-hasan-al-ash-ari.summary: Arab Muslim theologian (874-936) who founded the Ash'ari school of Sunni theology, steering a middle path between rationalist Mu'tazilism and traditionalist Atharism.

al-ghazali.name: Al-Ghazali
al-ghazali.summary: A Persian Sunni Muslim scholar and polymath (c. 1058-1111), regarded as one of Islamic history's most influential theologians, jurists and mystics.

tawhid.name: Tawhid
tawhid.summary: Islam's central concept of God's absolute oneness, forming the core of the Muslim declaration of faith and the foundation of Islamic theology.

yaqub-al-mansur.name: Ya'qub al-Mansur
yaqub-al-mansur.summary: Third Almohad caliph, reigning 1184 to 1199, whose rule saw flourishing trade, architecture, and scholarship alongside victories against the Reconquista in Iberia.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

isaac-ben-sheshet.name: Isaac ben Sheshet
isaac-ben-sheshet.summary: Spanish Talmudic authority (1326–1408), known by his acronym Rivash, who studied in Barcelona under Nissim of Gerona.

abdallah-ibn-yasin.name: Abdallah ibn Yasin
abdallah-ibn-yasin.summary: An Islamic theologian and spiritual leader, born in Tamanart, who founded the Almoravid movement and died in 1059.

sijilmasa.name: Sijilmasa
sijilmasa.summary: A medieval Moroccan trading city at the northern edge of the Sahara, an important terminus of trans-Saharan trade routes until the 14th century.

pope-gregory-vii.name: Pope Gregory VII
pope-gregory-vii.summary: Born Hildebrand of Sovana, head of the Catholic Church from 1073 to 1085; led the Gregorian Reform and clashed with Emperor Henry IV over papal authority.

hippo-regius.name: Hippo Regius
hippo-regius.summary: The ancient name of modern Annaba, Algeria, a city that served Phoenicians, Berbers, Romans and Vandals and was briefly the Vandal Kingdom's capital, and home to Augustine of Hippo.

african-romance.name: African Romance
african-romance.summary: An extinct Latin-derived Romance language spoken in Roman North Africa's coastal provinces, surviving under later Vandal, Byzantine and Berber rule into at least the 8th century, possibly much later.

nefzaoua.name: Nefzaoua
nefzaoua.summary: A region of southwest Tunisia, historically home to Christian Berbers later joined by Spanish Mozarab refugees fleeing the Reconquista.

jizya.name: Jizya
jizya.summary: Tax levied on non-Muslim subjects under Islamic law, historically understood as a fee for protection and exemption from military service.
